claims.text: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high or balanced mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperature, including approximately 1000 °C.
Reducing the Hf content by 20–30% and replacing it with Zr will lower the alloy density.
The Hf-reduced, Zr-enriched alloy can be prepared by arc melting followed by homogenization.
The modified alloy will remain a single-phase disordered solid solution.
The modified alloy will preserve substantial lattice distortion.
Hf and Zr are chemically similar and have comparable atomic radii.
Hf has a density of approximately 13.3 g/cm³.
Zr has a density of approximately 6.5 g/cm³.
Replacing Hf with Zr reduces average atomic mass and consequently reduces the alloy's overall density.
Chemical similarity between Hf and Zr will preserve solid-solution and lattice-distortion strengthening.
Preserved solid-solution and lattice-distortion strengthening will retain room-temperature and high-temperature mechanical performance.
The modified alloy will have a density approximately 10% or more below that of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain comparable yield strength and ductility at room temperature.
The modified alloy will retain comparable mechanical performance at approximately 1000 °C.
Reducing Hf may alter diffusion kinetics or microstructural stability at elevated temperatures.
The proposed performance boundary is room temperature through approximately 1000 °C under tensile and compressive loading analogous to that used for the baseline alloy.
The hypothesis is to be rejected if density falls by less than 5% or if yield strength or creep resistance at approximately 1000 °C degrades by more than approximately 15% relative to the control.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises no compromise and the prediction calls for comparable mechanical properties, but the rejection rule permits degradation of up to approximately 15% at 1000 °C without falsification.
The predicted density reduction is approximately 10% or more, whereas the hypothesis is rejected only below 5%; a 5–10% reduction would fail the stated prediction but would not trigger rejection.

The baseline is repeatedly defined as as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, but the experiment also says both samples receive identical homogenization procedures. A homogenized control is not strictly the stated as-cast baseline.
